standard.title: Innovation, enterprise and emerging technologies
standard.description: analyse the impact of innovation, enterprise and emerging technologies on designed solutions for global preferred futures
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse the impact of innovation and the development of technologies on designed solutions and sustainability (AC9TDE8K02). They can identify how innovation responds to community needs. They have not yet examined enterprise responses to technological change, used forecasting or backcasting techniques, or analysed innovation for global preferred futures.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how innovation, enterprise and emerging technologies interact to create designed solutions — and use forecasting and backcasting techniques to evaluate possible futures and their implications for society.

nodes.label: How enterprise responds to technological change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how commercial enterprises respond to the challenges and opportunities of technological change.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one way a commercial enterprise has responded to a technological change — either adapting an existing model or creating a new one; explain what drove the response.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how commercial enterprises respond to technological change — including changes to business models (e.g. e-commerce), carbon footprint considerations, and the competitive dynamics that drive innovation; examine at least two examples across different sectors.
wider: Compare how two enterprises in the same sector responded differently to the same technological shift — analyse why their responses differed and which was more effective
Investigate the carbon footprint implications of e-commerce compared with traditional retail — evaluate whether the convenience benefit is offset by the environmental cost
Examine how a First Nations enterprise has used emerging technology to scale, protect or commercialise traditional knowledge — for example, biodegradable polymers using spinifex grass

response_modes.reason: Enterprise response patterns need to accumulate across examples before students can reason about them — a single case study doesn't provide the range needed to apply enterprise thinking to novel futures. Multiple enterprise contexts build the schema that forecasting and backcasting can then work with.

success_criteria: Identifies a specific technological change and describes how an enterprise responded
Explains what drove the response (market opportunity, competitive pressure, regulation, etc.)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand how enterprises respond to technological change cannot productively apply forecasting and backcasting at N2 — the scenarios have no grounding in how real design and enterprise decisions are made.

nodes.label: Forecasting and backcasting for preferred futures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use forecasting and backcasting techniques to investigate possible futures and evaluate what opportunities and impacts they present.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe what forecasting and backcasting are; apply one technique to a scenario and describe one future implication.
nodes.typical_width: Apply forecasting (projecting current trends forward) and backcasting (starting from a preferred future and working backward) to a real-world challenge; identify opportunities and impacts for society and particular groups; explain what design or innovation decisions would be needed to move toward the preferred future.
wider: Apply backcasting to a specific global challenge (e.g. food security, clean energy access) — identify the design and technology decisions required at each stage to reach the preferred future
Investigate how the Asia region collaboration scenarios for designed solutions (e.g. collaborative design for pandemic response) used future-oriented thinking to define the problem
Compare forecasting and backcasting outputs for the same scenario — analyse what each technique reveals that the other doesn't

response_modes.reason: Forecasting and backcasting are reasoning techniques — students who don't apply a structured process produce vague futures rather than analysed scenarios. The scaffold (identify trend / preferred state → project or trace back → identify implications → identify design decisions) makes the technique productive.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Backcasting applied to real global challenges is genuinely rich — it connects design and technology decisions to consequential futures and requires students to reason across time and scales rather than describe a single innovation.
success_criteria: Applies at least one technique to a scenario and identifies at least one implication for society

nodes.label: Innovation from diverse knowledge systems
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how diverse knowledge systems — including First Nations knowledge — have led to innovative designed solutions.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one example of innovation that drew on a non-Western or First Nations knowledge system; explain what knowledge was applied and what problem it addressed.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how diverse knowledge systems have contributed to designed solutions — including First Nations Australian knowledges (e.g. spinifex biodegradable polymers), traditional ecological knowledge applied to contemporary materials, and cross-cultural design collaborations; evaluate how these contributions challenge assumptions about where innovation originates.
wider: Research how spinifex grass polymers are being developed as a sustainable material — analyse what First Nations knowledge was the foundation and what contemporary technology extended it

Investigate a real-world challenge in the Asia region where collaboration across knowledge systems produced a designed solution that a single knowledge system could not — explain what each system contributed
Examine how intellectual property frameworks interact with First Nations knowledge in design contexts — what protections exist and where gaps remain

response_modes.reason: Students often treat innovation as originating solely from Western science and technology. Diverse knowledge system examples — First Nations materials science, traditional ecological engineering, cross-cultural design — each challenge this assumption from a different angle and are better understood together than individually.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations materials science direction (spinifex polymers) is substantive and contemporary — it connects traditional knowledge to active research and commercialisation, making intellectual property and attribution questions genuinely significant.
success_criteria: Identifies a specific innovation and the knowledge system it drew on
Explains what aspect of that knowledge system enabled the innovation
